newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary says trade gap wider but acceptable.
newsitem.headline: Hungary says trade gap wider but acceptable.

text.p: Hungary's Ministry of Industry, Trade and Tourism (MIT) expects import growth to outstrip exports by about one percentage point this year but deems the gap is acceptable, a MIT official said on Thursday.
"This year we expect an export growth rate of 10 to 11 percent with imports growing about one percentage point faster," Lajos Berenyi, MIT Deputy Secretary of State told a news conference.
"As long as wages and consumption growth remains at a justifiable level, this should not be a cause for concern".
Berenyi said that according to preliminary figures Hungary's foreign trade deficit rose to $907 million in April from $690 million in March.
He added that although this would mean a proportional full-year trade gap of $2.7 billion, "(the ministry's) forecast of an $3 billion or somewhat higher trade gap is more realistic".
Imports growth outpaced exports by 1.7 percentage points in the January-April period compared with a 3.1 percentage point difference in the first quarter of this year, Berenyi said.
Imports rose by 12 percent, while exports increased by 10.3 percent in the first four months of the year compared with the same period of 1996.
Berenyi added that a 10 to 11 percent export growth rate could be sustained over the next two years if industrial output continues to grow at a seven percent rate.
He said export growth during the first four months was based on an industrial output rise of 7.2 percent.
"Economic performance is growing faster every month," Berenyi said.
He added that machinery exports rose by some 21 percent compared with the first four months of 1996 while the import of consumer goods was moderate.
"Consumer goods imports rose by a solid five percent," Berenyi said.

He also said that Hungary's export markets changed very little from last year with 78 percent going to developed countries, 19 percent towards central and east Europe and three percent into developing coutries.
Berenyi said Hungary's trade balance was moderately positive with its two main partners, Germany and Austria.

Exports to countries of the Central European Free Trade Agreement (CEFTA) registered the fastest growth with 27.5 percent but exports to Russia also showed dynamic growth, expanding by a rate of 15 to 16 percent, he said.
Of Hungary's four CEFTA partners, the trade balance was positive with Poland and Slovenia and showed a deficit with the Czech Republic and Slovakia, Berenyi said.
